description:
We are two engineers who share an interest in human spaceflight:
Shambhavi A S is an aerospace engineer who brings the mission and systems view: how spacecraft, habitats and crews work, and which hazards matter most.
Surabhi A S is a VLSI, embedded systems and medical electronics engineer who brings sensors, biomedical signals, low-level hardware and software.
For the "Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts" challenge, we have built a working prototype called SAMVIT.
summary: SAMVIT (Space Astronaut Monitoring, Vital Intelligence and Tracking) is a health monitor that helps astronauts assess their own health on long missions. It tracks heart rate, blood pressure, blood oxygen, temperature, glucose, mood, sleep, exercise and radiation dose, and judges each reading against that astronaut's own baseline for the activity they are doing. Readings are linked to NASA's five spaceflight hazards and eight Human Research Program risks, shown on a clickable body map with green, amber and red status. Astronauts can log their own readings, get due-now prompts, earn points and badges, and follow plain-language measurement guides. The app gives preventive actions, first-aid steps, a three-level escalation ladder to the flight surgeon with signal-delay awareness, and drills such as a solar particle event. It supports ISS, deep-space, lunar and Mars settings. Sensor feeds are simulated, this is not a medical device. SAMVIT matters because the crew must catch drift early when ground help is minutes away.
details:
SAMVIT is an astronaut health dashboard. Each simulated hour, every astronaut's suit reports vitals together with the activity before, during and after. Each reading is compared with the astronaut's expected value for that activity, so exercise is not an alarm, but slow recovery is flagged. Three detectors run together (an exponentially weighted average, a one-sided CUSUM and absolute clinical limits), and sensor checks flag stuck, noisy, impossible or lone-drifting readings. Indicator severities feed eight NASA-named risks, which feed the five hazards (radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, and hostile closed environment) and a Compound Hazard Index.

Features: Clickable body map with colour status, 72-hour trend charts with expected-versus-measured lines, habitat air and gravity readouts, manual vitals log with range checks, due-now prompts, points, streaks and badges, measurement guides, action cards for each flagged risk, pre-EVA readiness advice, a three-step escalation ladder with a signal-delay countdown, first-aid guides, voice and beep alerts, CSV, JSON and ground-brief export, a contactless camera pulse scan, and an offline assistant (with an optional online mode using the user's own API key). Settings: ISS, deep-space transit, lunar base, Mars habitat.

Benefits and impact. Astronauts get a quick, readable picture of their health and a clear next step, which matters when ground contact is delayed. Gamification and prompts make routine checks a habit.

Tools. Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript in one file, inline SVG, the Web Speech and Web Audio APIs, and the browser camera API.

Limits. Sensor feeds are simulated, risk weights are illustrative, bone and immune statuses are proxies, the camera pulse is sensitive to light, motion and skin tone. Not a medical device. Actions contain no drug doses.
